paragraphs.heading: The first billion years
paragraphs.text: Early Earth, sometimes called Proto-Earth, is a loose label for the planet's first billion years, a span also called a gigayear and written Ga. It starts when Earth took shape in the young Solar System, about 4.55 billion years ago, and runs to the close of the Eoarchean era, near 3.5 billion years ago. On the geologic time scale, that covers the whole Hadean eon plus roughly a third of the Archean eon that came next.

paragraphs.heading: How fast did Earth build
paragraphs.text: The planet grew out of the solar nebula through a process called accretion. Radiometric dating and other evidence place its birth about 4.54 billion years ago. The leading theory says a planet like ours takes some 50 to 100 million years to form, but newer ideas have kept planetary scientists debating. In June 2023 one team reported evidence that Earth may have come together in just three million years. A later study found that its chemical ingredients were fixed within about 3 million years, as the protoplanetary disk thinned out, while the full build-up was finished within about 70 million years.

paragraphs.heading: Collisions and the Moon
paragraphs.text: This was a time of violent impacts. The young planet, a protoplanet with about 0.63 of today's Earth mass, was starting to sweep its orbital path clear. One collision was with Theia, a body the size of Mars that shared Earth's orbit and was probably nudged out of the L₄ Lagrange point. That crash, which formed the Moon about 0.032 Ga after the Solar System formed, left behind a series of magma oceans and bouts of core formation. Once the core had formed, meteorites or comets from the outer Solar System may have brought water and other volatile compounds in a heavy bombardment known as the late veneer.

paragraphs.heading: From lava world to ocean world
paragraphs.text: Earth's first air was mostly hydrogen and helium, gathered from the protoplanetary disk. It gave way to a second, reducing atmosphere rich in nitrogen, methane and CO₂. Toward the end of the Hadean the surface cooled and a stable crust formed. Most of the water vapor then fell out of the air into a superocean that covered almost the entire planet. The lava planet of the Hadean had become an ocean planet by the early Archean, and the earliest known life showed up soon after.

paragraphs.heading: What the rocks still hold
paragraphs.text: Very little crust from this time has survived. The oldest dated piece is a grain of the mineral zircon, 4.404 ± 0.008 billion years old, sealed inside a metamorphosed sandstone conglomerate in the Jack Hills of Western Australia. Supracrustal terrains such as the Isua greenstone belt, the earliest of their kind, date from the second half of the period, about 3.8 billion years ago. That is close to the peak of the Late Heavy Bombardment.

paragraphs.heading: The first signs of life
paragraphs.text: Before the first billion years were over, life had appeared in the oceans and begun to change the air and the surface, helping both aerobic and anaerobic organisms to spread. Life on Earth goes back at least 3.5 billion years. Possible older traces include graphite, perhaps made by living things, in 3.7-billion-year-old metasedimentary rocks from southwestern Greenland, and zircon grains 4.1 billion years old from Western Australia. In November 2020 an international team reported that Earth's earliest atmosphere was probably very unlike the conditions assumed in the Miller–Urey studies of how life began.
